name: Communication Forensics
title: Communication Forensics
answer: Communication forensics is the examination of messages, calls, emails and documents to establish who said what, when, and whether the record can be trusted. In fraud and forensic accounting it covers the review of email threads, chat logs, call detail records and voicemail, often to reconstruct an instruction, an approval or a concealment. It also covers the authenticity of a document itself, including whether a message was altered, backdated or generated by a machine rather than a person. The work sits between accounting, investigation and dispute support, and it usually begins when a transaction, a payment or a disclosure is questioned.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Communication forensics is the examination of messages, calls, emails and documents to establish who said what, when, and whether the record can be trusted. In fraud and forensic accounting it covers the review of email threads, chat logs, call detail records and voicemail, often to reconstruct an instruction, an approval or a concealment. It also covers the authenticity of a document itself, including whether a message was altered, backdated or generated by a machine rather than a person. The work sits between accounting, investigation and dispute support, and it usually begins when a transaction, a payment or a disclosure is questioned.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Practitioners work from preserved copies rather than live mailboxes, using forensic images of devices, server-side journaling and exports from collaboration platforms. Common tools include email review platforms for search and threading, mobile extraction kits for handsets, and call detail record analysis for telecom data. Audio work relies on speech-to-text and speaker separation, and document work relies on metadata inspection and file comparison. Storage and processing are usually handled in a controlled review environment so that the original evidence stays untouched.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with a defined question, such as who authorised a transfer or whether a signature block was reused. Investigators collect and hash the material, then index it so that searches, date filters and participant filters can be applied consistently. Threads are reconstructed into conversations, and gaps, deletions and out-of-sequence timestamps are flagged. Language models and transcription tools speed up triage and translation, but findings are verified against the underlying message or recording before they are reported. The output is a chronology with citations to specific items, not a summary of impressions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Communication records carry privacy, employment and data protection obligations that vary by jurisdiction, and collection must stay within the authority the matter provides. Chain of custody, hashing and documented handling keep the material admissible and defensible if the matter reaches a regulator or a court. Where AI tools are used for review or transcription, the model, version and settings should be recorded so the process can be reproduced. Findings are evidence for a qualified investigator or counsel to weigh, and this page describes practice rather than giving legal advice on any specific matter.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The volume and variety of channels keeps growing, so review increasingly depends on automated triage to decide what a human reads closely. Synthetic text, cloned voices and edited audio raise the bar for authenticity testing, and detection methods are being folded into standard examination steps. Regulators and courts are asking more precise questions about how AI-assisted review was configured and checked. The likely direction is tighter documentation of tooling and provenance alongside the traditional chain of custody, so that a finding can be traced from a conclusion back to an unaltered original.
